summary:
FieldTwin is a geospatial decision-support prototype for identifying Earth terrain that could serve as a test analog for locations on Mars. Our long-term vision is simple: a researcher selects a location on Mars, and FieldTwin searches Earth elevation datasets, compares measurable terrain properties, and returns ranked candidate analogs with explanations and uncertainty.

As a reproducible proof of concept, we combined NASADEM elevation data for Chile’s Atacama Desert with a USGS Mars CTX digital terrain model and NASA PDS MOLA context. We evaluated six Earth sites using slope, local relief, and surface roughness at two analysis scales. An interpretable, unweighted Pareto comparison found four nondominated candidates, but no single scientifically validated winner. We also tested numerical rover routes and the sensitivity of results to hypothetical elevation perturbations.

The public prototype enables users to explore the documented sites, inspect evidence and trade-offs, and understand which Earth–Mars properties cannot be directly transferred. FieldTwin’s goal is to make planetary analog screening more transparent, reproducible, and useful for planning future rover navigation experiments—not to claim that a suitable Mars analog has already been proven.
details:
Vision and Current Scope

FieldTwin is an evidence-based geospatial research prototype for comparing the terrain of a documented Martian reference with candidate Earth locations. Its long-term vision is a platform where a researcher selects any location on Mars, triggers a search across Earth terrain datasets, and receives transparent, ranked candidate analogs.

The submitted prototype demonstrates the scientific workflow on a bounded Atacama Desert case study; it does not yet implement arbitrary Mars-point selection or worldwide Earth search.

How the Prototype Works

1. Data acquisition and provenance

We used NASADEM_HGT.001 elevation data from NASA’s LP DAAC for Earth, a USGS CTX stereo-derived digital terrain model as the provisional local Mars reference, and NASA PDS MOLA data for broad Martian topographic context. Our source inventory records product identifiers, geographic scope, coordinate systems, and checksums.

2. Physically interpretable terrain analysis

Our Python pipeline processes Earth and Mars elevations in their respective planetary coordinate systems and extracts terrain patches on a 100 m computational grid, using 1 km and 2 km analysis windows.

It measures three physical characteristics:

  • Plane-fit slope (degrees).
  • P95–P05 local relief (meters).
  • Plane-detrended RMS surface roughness (meters).

A common analysis grid does not mean that the source datasets have identical effective accuracy or resolution.

3. Transparent candidate comparisons

We evaluated six Earth sites: four Atacama pilot candidates, an ARADS Playa point representing historical regional analog activity, and a rugged Láscar volcanic comparison.

We minimized the absolute difference between Mars and Earth for each of the three descriptors using unweighted Pareto nondominated sorting, not a single similarity percentage.

Four pilots were nondominated at both tested scales, with no unique validated winner.

4. Numerical rover-route experiments and uncertainty

We conducted 60 digital-elevation-model route searches using distance-only and hypothetical 3-degree/10-degree grade constraints. We also stress-tested rankings and route behavior under assumed elevation perturbations.

These are computational experiments, not physical rover trials or calibrated mission-safety probabilities.

Exploratory machine-learning models were also benchmarked. They did not establish scientifically validated superiority to the physical baseline, which remains our primary comparison method.

The Interactive Experience

Our React and TypeScript website offers four connected sections: Mission, Earth Search, Comparison, and Transfer/Rover Test.

Visitors can inspect six mapped locations, switch map layers and analysis windows, compare feature differences and Pareto fronts, review uncertainty, and see which analog properties could or could not transfer to a rover experiment.

The browser presents precomputed, documented scientific results rather than conducting new DEM processing.

Technology and Creativity

We used Python, NumPy, Rasterio, and other scientific and geospatial libraries for terrain processing; scikit-learn for exploratory ML experiments; React, TypeScript, Vite, and MapLibre GL JS for the user interface; OpenStreetMap, OpenTopoMap, and NASA GIBS for geographic context; and GitHub Pages for deployment.

Our distinctive contribution is an auditable decision process connecting planetary terrain data, multi-objective comparisons, numerical navigation experiments, and explicit limits on analog transfer.

Rather than assuming that visually similar terrain guarantees similar rover performance, FieldTwin distinguishes measurable topographic similarities from environmental and engineering properties requiring independent evidence.

Benefits, Intended Impact, and Future Development

FieldTwin could eventually help mission teams, robotics laboratories, and planetary researchers prioritize terrestrial sites for rover-navigation studies, reduce preliminary screening effort, and target follow-up surveys.

Scaling the platform requires broader Earth coverage, user-selected Martian targets, independent CTX quality assessment, rover-specific operating constraints, geological and soil evidence, and physical field validation.

Our completed work establishes a reproducible exploratory comparison, not certification of a field site, discovery of a new analog, or demonstration of physical rover performance.

Source code, scientific methods, and supporting evidence:

https://github.com/SamaBeyond/fieldtwin
